noteRef.topicTitle: 1. Structure, Bonding & Introduction to Organic Chemistry

specPoints.text: be able to use chemical equations to calculate volumes of gases and vice versa, using: i the concepts of amount of substance ii the molar volume of gases iii the expression pV = n RT for gases and volatile liquids

primer.text: Gases are the forgiving state: any mole of any gas claims the same volume. This note fixes the 24.0 dm3 room-condition and 22.4 dm3 standard-condition values, chains gas volumes through equation ratios, then extends to any conditions with the ideal gas expression pV = nRT and its SI unit discipline.

lessons.title: Molar gas volumes
lessons.opening: Under the same conditions, one mole of any gas claims the same volume. This lesson pins the 24.0 dm^3 r.t.p. and 22.4 dm^3 s.t.p. values, converts volumes to moles and back, and chains gas volumes through equation ratios.
keyPoints: At r.t.p. (293 K, 101.3 kPa) the molar gas volume is 24.0 dm^3; at s.t.p. (273 K) it is 22.4 dm^3.
Moles of gas = volume in dm^3 / molar gas volume.
Gas volumes scale with equation ratios: 6.50 dm^3 of propane yields 45.5 dm^3 of total gaseous products.
Volume foresight sizes the equipment for gas-evolving experiments.

low.restatement: Divide the gas volume by 24.0 (room conditions) to get moles, or multiply moles by 24.0 to predict the volume.
low.analogy: Every gas fills a same-sized apartment at room conditions; moles count apartments occupied.
low.examPointer: State which conditions you are using - the 24.0 vs 22.4 choice is itself a mark.

medium.restatement: Because equal volumes hold equal numbers of gas particles (Avogadro's law), the equation's mole ratio applies directly to volumes at fixed temperature and pressure, even between different gases.
medium.analogy: Gas volumes behave like identical train carriages: the ratio of carriages needed is the ratio written in the equation.
medium.examPointer: For propane C3H8 + 5O2 -> 3CO2 + 4H2O (steam), each 1 volume of propane gives 7 volumes of gaseous product - 6.50 x 7 = 45.5 dm^3.

check.stem: What is the molar gas volume at room temperature and pressure?

options.explanation: At 293 K and 101.3 kPa, one mole of any gas occupies 24.0 dm^3.
That is the s.t.p. value at 273 K.
The unit is dm^3, a thousand times larger.
That is far too small for a mole of gas.

check.stem: How many moles occupy 4.5 dm^3 of carbon dioxide at r.t.p.?

options.explanation: That uses the s.t.p. divisor 22.4.
That inverts the division.
The volume is not itself a mole count.

check.stem: Why is the gas identity irrelevant when converting volume to moles at fixed conditions?

options.text: Equal volumes of any gases contain equal numbers of particles under the same conditions
options.explanation: Avogadro's law makes the volume-per-mole universal.

options.text: Because all gases have identical molar masses
options.explanation: Molar masses differ; the volume law does not depend on them.
Most laboratory gases are compounds.

options.text: Because volume never depends on temperature
options.explanation: Volume responds strongly to temperature.

check.stem: 1.50 g of sodium (Ar 23.0) reacts with water at s.t.p. What volume of hydrogen evolves?

options.explanation: n(Na) = 0.0652 mol; ratio 2:1 gives 0.0326 mol H2; V = 0.0326 mol on 22.4 dm^3 per mol gives 0.730 dm^3.
That forgot the 2:1 ratio halving.
That halved twice.
That assumes a full mole of hydrogen.

check.stem: 6.50 dm^3 of propane burns completely: C3H8 + 5O2 -> 3CO2 + 4H2O (steam). What total gas volume forms?

options.explanation: Each propane volume gives 3 + 4 = 7 volumes of gaseous product: 6.50 x 7 = 45.5 dm^3.
That counted only the carbon dioxide.
That used the 5-volume oxygen coefficient.
Conservation of gas volume does not hold when molecule counts change.

check.stem: State the molar gas volumes at r.t.p. and s.t.p. with their condition definitions.
check.modelAnswer: At r.t.p. (293 K / 20 degrees C, 101.3 kPa) the molar gas volume is 24.0 dm^3; at s.t.p. (273 K / 0 degrees C, 101.3 kPa) it is 22.4 dm^3.

check.stem: State the equation linking moles of gas to its volume at fixed conditions.
check.modelAnswer: Moles of gas = volume of gas in dm^3 / molar gas volume in dm^3.

check.stem: Explain why gas volumes can pass straight through an equation's ratio while masses cannot.
check.modelAnswer: At fixed temperature and pressure, equal volumes contain equal numbers of gas particles, so a volume ratio between gases IS a mole ratio; masses require conversion through each substance's molar mass because a gram of one gas is not a gram's worth of formula units of another.

check.stem: Calculate the volume of hydrogen, at s.t.p., released when 1.50 g of sodium reacts fully with water, quoting every step.
check.modelAnswer: 2Na + 2H2O -> 2NaOH + H2; n(Na) = 1.50 / 23.0 = 0.0652 mol; ratio 2:1 gives 0.0326 mol H2; V = 0.0326 mol on 22.4 dm^3 per mol gives 0.730 dm^3 (3 s.f.).

lessons.title: The ideal gas expression
lessons.opening: Away from room conditions, pV = nRT takes over. This lesson states the kinetic theory assumptions behind 'ideal', fixes the SI unit discipline (Pa, m^3, K), and extracts both volumes and molar masses from the expression.
keyPoints: Ideal gases follow kinetic theory: fast random motion, negligible particle volume, no intermolecular forces, elastic collisions.
pV = nRT uses pressure in Pa, volume in m^3, temperature in K, and R = 8.31 J K^-1 mol^-1.
Rearranging gives volumes (V = nRT/p) or moles (n = pV/RT) or molar masses.
kPa multiply by 1000 for Pa; cm^3 divide by 10^6 for m^3; Celsius add 273 for K.

low.restatement: Pressure times volume equals moles times gas constant times temperature; three of the four quantities decide the fourth.
low.analogy: It is a four-way seesaw: squeeze the volume and the pressure rises; heat it and either pressure or volume must grow.
low.examPointer: The Data Booklet supplies R; your job is the SI conversions and the rearrangement.

medium.restatement: The expression derives from kinetic theory: particle impacts create pressure, so pV scales with the particle count n and their average kinetic energy, which temperature measures.
medium.analogy: Pressure is the drumbeat of molecules on the walls - more molecules (n) or faster ones (T) beat louder (p).
medium.examPointer: Real gases only approximate ideal behaviour; exam data are chosen so the deviation is negligible.

check.stem: Which unit set does the ideal gas expression pV = nRT demand?

options.text: Pa, m^3, mol, K with R = 8.31 J K^-1 mol^-1
options.explanation: Those are the SI pairings the gas constant is calibrated for.

options.text: kPa, dm^3, mol, degrees C with R = 8.31
options.explanation: Those mixed units contradict the constant's calibration.
Another non-SI blend requiring different R.
Volume must be m^3, not cm^3.

check.stem: What are the kinetic theory's core assumptions?

options.text: Fast random motion, negligible particle volume, no intermolecular forces, elastic collisions
options.explanation: Those four assumptions define the ideal gas model.

options.text: Heavy particles, strong attractions, slow motion
options.explanation: That is the opposite of the model.

options.text: Fixed particle volume and inelastic collisions
options.explanation: Both violate the ideal assumptions.
Temperature is one consequence; the assumption list is longer.

check.stem: Calculate the volume of 0.781 mol of oxygen at 220 kPa and 21 degrees C.

options.explanation: The m^3-to-dm^3 conversion was missed.
The conversion multiplied by 10^5 instead of 10^3.
The final unit is dm^3 after conversion.

check.stem: A 1000 cm^3 flask at 300 kPa and 23 degrees C holds 6.39 g of a gas. What is its molar mass?

options.explanation: A factor of ten slipped in the moles.
The division inverted.
Mass is not itself a molar mass.

check.stem: Why does the ideal gas equation still serve real gases well in exam calculations?

options.text: Real gases come very close to ideal behaviour under ordinary conditions
options.explanation: Deviations shrink at low pressure and moderate temperature, so the model predicts well.

options.text: Because real gases have no intermolecular forces at all
options.explanation: They do; the forces are just small enough to neglect.

options.text: Because R is re-measured for each gas
options.explanation: R is universal.
Units are precisely where marks live.

check.stem: State the ideal gas equation with every variable's unit.
check.modelAnswer: pV = nRT with pressure in Pa, volume in m^3, n in mol, R = 8.31 J K^-1 mol^-1 and temperature in K.

check.stem: State the three unit conversions pV = nRT calculations typically need.
check.modelAnswer: kPa to Pa multiply by 1000; cm^3 to m^3 multiply by 10^-6; Celsius to Kelvin add 273.

check.stem: Explain why temperature must enter in Kelvin, not Celsius.
check.modelAnswer: The equation tracks average kinetic energy, which starts from absolute zero - the total cessation of particle motion; Celsius zero is an arbitrary ice point, so using it would treat a 273 K energy floor as if it were nothing, collapsing the proportionality.

check.stem: A flask of 1000 cm^3 holds 6.39 g of gas at 300 kPa and 23 degrees C. Use pV = nRT to find its relative molecular mass.

glossary.definition: The volume one mole of any gas occupies at stated conditions: 24.0 dm^3 at r.t.p., 22.4 dm^3 at s.t.p.
A gas obeying the kinetic theory assumptions and pV = nRT exactly.
The model of fast, randomly moving, volume-less particles colliding elastically, with temperature measuring average kinetic energy.

workedExample.prompt: Find the volume that 0.781 mol of oxygen claims at 220 kPa and 21 degrees C.
steps: Convert: 220 kPa = 220000 Pa; 21 degrees C = 294 K.
